text: Every .py file you've saved so far is technically a module. This lesson covers import, a few standard-library modules you'll genuinely use -- math, statistics, random, os -- and what a package is, which is the piece that makes pandas and every other library in this course available at all.

import math makes everything inside the math module available under the name math-dot -- so math.sqrt is the sqrt function that lives inside math, not something you wrote yourself. If you only need one or two things, from math import sqrt, ceil pulls them in directly, skipping the prefix. This course generally keeps the math. prefix, since it makes it obvious at a glance where a function came from.

statistics.mean and statistics.median summarize a batch of numbers in one line each. This is exactly the kind of number you'll compute constantly once you're working with real batches of records -- a small, hand-built preview of what pandas's describe method will do automatically, at a much larger scale, starting in Chapter 4.

random.choice picks one item from a list; random.shuffle reorders it in place -- useful once you start generating realistic test data without a real production source. os.getcwd tells you where your script is actually running from, and os.path.exists checks whether a file is really there before you try to open it, a check you'll lean on constantly starting in Lesson 13.

A package is a folder of related modules, usually downloaded from the Python Package Index with pip, Python's package installer. Once installed, you import it exactly like a standard-library module -- import pandas as pd is the line you'll write at the top of nearly every script from Chapter 4 onward, with as pd creating a shorter alias. The standard-library modules in this lesson need no pip install at all; third-party packages like pandas do.
Next up: list and dict comprehensions -- building a new list or dictionary from an existing one in a single readable line, instead of a multi-line loop.
